# How to use this guide

Pharmacy Law and Ethics (ER20-26T) is a second-year D.Pharm theory subject of **75 hours**, with no practical. The syllabus has **21 short chapters**. Chapter 3 (Drugs and Cosmetics Act and Rules) alone has 23 hours, so this guide splits it into two units; many 1- and 2-hour chapters are joined so that each unit is a sensible study block.

| Guide unit | Syllabus chapter(s) | Hours in syllabus |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1. General principles of law, history and Acts | 1 | 2 |
| 2. Pharmacy Act 1948 and Pharmacy Practice Regulations 2015 | 2 | 5 |
| 3. Drugs and Cosmetics Act – objectives, definitions, schedules, import, administration | 3 (part) | 23 (shared) |
| 4. Drugs and Cosmetics Act – manufacture, schedules, sale, records, banned drugs | 3 (part) | (shared) |
| 5. NDPS Act 1985 and Poisons Act 1919 | 4 and 7 | 2 + 2 |
| 6. Drugs and Magic Remedies Act 1954 and Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act 1960 | 5 and 6 | 2 + 2 |
| 7. NPPA, DPCO 2013, Pharmaceutical Policy 2002 and NLEM | 9 | 5 |
| 8. Code of Pharmaceutical Ethics | 10 | 5 |
| 9. FSSAI and food supplements, MTP Act, Clinical Establishments Act | 8, 11 and 16 | 2 + 2 + 2 |
| 10. CDSCO and IPC, good regulatory practices, medical devices | 12, 13 and 21 | 1 + 3 + 2 |
| 11. New drug development, clinical trials, BCS, ANDA/NDA, brands, patents, EUA | 14 | 7 |
| 12. Blood bank and Bio-Medical Waste Management Rules 2016 | 15 and 17 | 2 + 2 |
| 13. Bioethics and ICMR guidelines, Consumer Protection Act, Disaster Management Act | 18, 19 and 20 | 2 + 1 + 1 |

Suggested order: Units 2, 3, 4 and 8 first (they carry the most marks), then 5, 7 and 11, then the rest. Read a unit, close the notes, write the "Remember" points from memory, then answer that unit's questions.

## Exam pattern (ER-2020 theory paper)

D.Pharm ER-2020 examinations are yearly. In Himachal Pradesh the board (HPTSB) conducts them under the PCI ER-2020 scheme. The theory paper is **80 marks, 3 hours**; another 20 marks come from sessional (internal) assessment. The usual paper looks like this; **confirm the exact pattern with your college**, because boards sometimes change the format.

| Section | What it asks | Marks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| I | Objective questions (MCQs / one-word / fill in the blanks) – all compulsory | 20 × 1 = 20 |
| II | Short answers – attempt 10 of 11 | 10 × 3 = 30 |
| III | Long answers – attempt 6 of 7 | 6 × 5 = 30 |

In this guide **long** questions are 5-mark answers and **short** questions are 3-mark answers, to match this pattern. **Very-short** (2-mark) questions are included for quick revision and sessional tests.

## Probability ratings

- **High** – asked in most years; prepare the full answer.
- **Medium** – asked every few years or as part of a bigger question.
- **Low** – rare, but useful for MCQs and as a backup choice.

Ratings are an estimate from syllabus weight and the kind of questions usually set in D.Pharm papers. They are not a promise.

## Laws change – how to handle it in the exam

- Fines, form numbers, schedule contents and fees are revised often. This guide gives figures only where they are well established, and otherwise says "check the current rules".
- In the exam, write the **name of the Act and year**, the **objective**, the **authority** and the **key provision** correctly; that earns most marks. If you mention an amendment (for example, MTP Amendment 2021, NDCT Rules 2019, Medical Devices Rules 2017), give its year.
- If your teacher gives you a newer figure from an official notification, use it.

## Scoring tips for Pharmacy Law and Ethics

1. **Start every answer with the full name and year of the law**, then its **objectives**. Examiners look for this first.
2. **Definitions carry marks.** Learn the exact meaning of drug, cosmetic, misbranded, adulterated, spurious, patent or proprietary medicine, magic remedy, narcotic drug, psychotropic substance, ceiling price, scheduled formulation, registered pharmacist.
3. **Use tables** for constitution of PCI and State Councils, DTAB vs DCC, licence forms, schedules with labels, BMW colour codes, BCS classes, NDA vs ANDA, brand vs generic.
4. **Draw a simple flow chart** for the administration of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, the drug development process, or BMW handling – it makes the answer clear and quick to mark.
5. **For a 5-mark answer**, write about one and a half pages: definition/objective, a table or classification, 5–6 explained points, and a one-line conclusion.
6. **For a 3-mark answer**, write 5–6 crisp points or a small table.
7. **Ethics answers**: use the four headings – in relation to his **job**, **trade**, **medical profession** and **profession** – with 3–4 points under each.
8. **Do not invent numbers.** A correct principle without a figure is better than a wrong figure.

# Last-night revision sheet

If you have only a few hours, master these: **PCI constitution and functions**, **State Pharmacy Council and registration**, **D&C Act definitions (misbranded, adulterated, spurious)**, **DTAB, DCC, CDL and drug inspectors**, **licence forms and schedules (C, C1, G, H, H1, K, M, N, P, X)**, **NDPS definitions and penalties**, **DMR Act prohibited and exempted advertisements**, **DPCO 2013 ceiling price and NLEM**, **code of ethics (job, trade, medical profession, profession)**, **BMW colour coding**, **clinical trial phases and BCS**.

## NDPS and Poisons (Unit 5)

- Narcotic drug = coca leaf, cannabis, opium, poppy straw, manufactured drugs. Charas = resin; ganja = flowering tops.
- UN conventions 1961, 1971, 1988. Authorities: Narcotics Commissioner, NCB.
- Small quantity: up to 1 year RI or ₹10,000; intermediate: up to 10 years + ₹1 lakh; commercial: 10–20 years RI + ₹1–2 lakh.
- Poisons Act: Centre controls import; States control possession and sale; poison register.

## Advertisements and animals (Unit 6)

- DMR Act bans ads for: miscarriage/contraception, sexual capacity, menstrual disorders, Schedule diseases; misleading ads; magic remedies (talisman, mantra, kavacha, charm).
- Exempt: RMP signboard, scientific book, confidential to RMPs, Government ads, ads with Government sanction.
- PCA Act: CPCSEA; IAEC with CPCSEA nominee; animals from registered breeders; 3Rs.

## Prices (Unit 7)

- DPCO 2013 under Essential Commodities Act 1955; NPPA enforces.
- Scheduled formulation = NLEM medicine. Ceiling price = average PTR (brands ≥1% share) + 16%.
- Yearly WPI revision; non-scheduled up to 10% a year. NLEM 2022 = 384 medicines (P, S, T).

## Ethics (Unit 8)

Job (scope, conduct of pharmacy, prescriptions, drugs, apprentices) · Trade (fair price, fair trading, genuine purchase, no hawking, dignified ads) · Medical profession (no diagnosis/prescribing, no clandestine arrangements, liaison) · Profession (vigilance, law-abiding, associations, decorum) · Oath.

questions.answer:
1. Law: rules made by a recognised authority that everyone must follow; breach is punished by courts.
2. Sources: (a) Constitution – supreme law, divides law-making power into Union, State and Concurrent Lists; drugs and poisons and the professions are in the Concurrent List; (b) legislation – Acts of Parliament or State Legislatures (Pharmacy Act 1948); (c) delegated legislation – rules, regulations, orders made under an Act (Drugs and Cosmetics Rules 1945); (d) judicial precedent – decisions of higher courts; (e) custom.
3. Act: passed by the legislature; gives objectives, definitions, authorities, prohibitions and penalties (Drugs and Cosmetics Act 1940).
4. Rules: made by the Government under power given by the Act; give procedures, forms, fees, licence conditions and schedules (Drugs and Cosmetics Rules 1945).
5. Regulations: made by a statutory body with Government approval for its own field (Education Regulations 2020, Pharmacy Practice Regulations 2015 made by PCI).
6. Orders and notifications: specific controls issued under an Act, e.g. DPCO 2013 under the Essential Commodities Act; schedules can be changed by notification.

3. Drugs Act 1940 (later Drugs and Cosmetics Act) and Rules 1945: control of import, manufacture, distribution and sale.
4. Pharmacy Act 1948: PCI (1949) and State Councils, education standards and registration.

questions.answer:
1. A draft Bill is prepared by the concerned ministry.
2. Introduced in one House of Parliament: first reading (introduction), second reading (general discussion and clause-by-clause consideration, may be sent to a committee), third reading (passed).
3. The same process in the other House; differences are settled.
4. President's assent – the Bill becomes an Act.
5. Published in the Gazette; comes into force on the date notified; sections may start on different dates.
6. Later changes by amendment Acts; repeal removes an Act.
7. Constitutional basis: Seventh Schedule – Union, State and Concurrent Lists; drugs and poisons and medical and other professions are in the Concurrent List, so Parliament makes central drug laws while States enforce many parts (sale licences, pharmacy councils).

# Unit 1: General principles of law, history and Acts related to drugs and pharmacy

This unit covers syllabus chapter 1. It explains what law is, how an Act is made in India, the difference between an Act, Rules and Regulations, and how the laws that control medicines and the pharmacy profession grew over time. Read it first: every later unit uses these words.

## 1.1 What law is and why pharmacy needs it

**Law** is a set of rules made by a recognised authority (Parliament, a State Legislature or a body given power by them) that everyone must follow. Breaking it leads to a penalty imposed by a court.

Medicines are different from ordinary goods:

- The buyer (the patient) cannot judge their quality by looking at them.
- A wrong, fake or poor-quality medicine can cause harm or death.
- Some medicines (narcotics, sedatives) can be misused and cause addiction.
- Prices and supply of essential medicines affect public health.

So the State controls who may make, import, store, sell and dispense medicines, and who may practise as a pharmacist. **Pharmaceutical jurisprudence** is the branch of law that deals with these controls.

## 1.2 Sources of law in India

| Source | Meaning | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Constitution of India | The supreme law; every other law must agree with it | Division of law-making power between Union and States |
| Legislation (statutes) | Acts passed by Parliament or a State Legislature | Pharmacy Act, 1948 |
| Delegated (subordinate) legislation | Rules, regulations, orders and notifications made by the Government or a body under the power given by an Act | Drugs Rules, 1945; Pharmacy Practice Regulations, 2015 |
| Judicial precedent | Earlier decisions of the Supreme Court and High Courts that later courts follow | Interpretation of "drug" or "patent" in a case |
| Custom | Long-followed practice accepted as binding | Rarely important in drug law |

### The Constitution and drug law

The Seventh Schedule of the Constitution divides subjects into three lists:

- **Union List** – only Parliament makes laws (for example, import and export across customs frontiers, patents).
- **State List** – only States make laws (for example, public health, hospitals and dispensaries).
- **Concurrent List** – both may make laws; if they conflict, the Union law usually prevails. **"Drugs and poisons"** and **"legal, medical and other professions"** are in the Concurrent List.

This is why the main drug laws are Central Acts, but their day-to-day enforcement (sale licences, drug inspectors at district level, pharmacy councils) is done by the States.

## 1.3 Act, Rules, Regulations and Orders

| Term | Who makes it | What it contains |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Act** (statute) | Parliament or State Legislature | The main law: objectives, definitions, authorities, prohibitions, offences and penalties |
| **Rules** | Central or State Government, under a section of the Act | Detailed procedures: forms, fees, licence conditions, labelling, schedules |
| **Regulations** | A statutory body (for example, PCI) with the Government's approval | Standards for its own area, such as education or practice |
| **Order** | Government under an Act | A specific control, such as the Drugs (Prices Control) Order, 2013 under the Essential Commodities Act |
| **Notification** | Government, published in the Official Gazette | Brings a rule into force, bans a drug, adds a drug to a schedule |

**Schedules** are lists attached to an Act or to Rules (for example, Schedule H of the Drugs Rules). They can be changed by notification without passing a new Act, so they change often.

## 1.4 How an Act is made

```text
Draft Bill (Ministry)
      |
      v
Introduced in one House of Parliament
      |
First reading -> Second reading (clause-by-clause, may go to a Committee) -> Third reading (passed)
      |
      v
Same process in the other House
      |
      v
President's assent  -->  Act
      |
      v
Published in the Gazette of India; comes into force on the date notified
```

- A **Bill** becomes an **Act** only after both Houses pass it and the President gives assent.
- An Act may come into force at once or on a date the Government notifies. Different sections can start on different dates.
- An **amendment Act** changes an existing Act. A **repeal** removes an Act; usually a newer Act replaces it.

## 1.5 Some basic legal terms

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Offence | An act or omission that the law punishes |
| Cognizable offence | Police may arrest without a warrant |
| Bailable / non-bailable | Whether bail is a right or at the court's discretion |
| Licence | Written permission from an authority to do something that is otherwise prohibited (manufacture, sale) |
| Licensee | The holder of a licence |
| Penalty | Punishment: fine, imprisonment or both, and sometimes confiscation |
| Compounding | Settling certain minor offences by paying an amount instead of trial |
| Ex officio | Holding a post because of another office (for example, the Drugs Controller General as a member of a board) |
| Gazette notification | Official publication that gives legal effect to rules and orders |

**Civil law** deals with disputes between persons (contracts, compensation). **Criminal law** deals with offences against society, such as selling spurious drugs. Most drug laws create criminal offences.

## 1.6 History of drug and pharmacy law in India

### Before the main Acts

- In the 19th and early 20th centuries most modern medicines were imported. There was no control over their quality, and many sub-standard and adulterated products were sold.
- Opium was controlled mainly for revenue, through the **Opium Acts of 1857 and 1878**.
- The **Poisons Act, 1919** regulated the possession and sale of poisons.
- The **Dangerous Drugs Act, 1930** controlled opium, coca leaf, cannabis and their products.

### Drugs Enquiry Committee (Chopra Committee), 1930–31

The Government of India appointed this committee under **Col. R. N. Chopra** to study the sale of drugs and the state of pharmacy in India. Its main findings and advice:

1. Poor-quality and adulterated drugs were widely sold; a central law was needed to control the import, manufacture, distribution and sale of drugs.
2. A central drugs laboratory should test drugs.
3. India should have its own pharmacopoeia.
4. Pharmacists should be properly trained and registered; a law should regulate the profession.

Its report led to the **Drugs Act, 1940** and later the **Pharmacy Act, 1948**.

### After independence

| Year | Law or event | Main purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1919 | Poisons Act | Possession, sale and import of poisons |
| 1940 | Drugs Act (later extended to cosmetics and renamed the Drugs and Cosmetics Act) | Quality control of drugs: import, manufacture, distribution, sale |
| 1945 | Drugs Rules (now Drugs and Cosmetics Rules) | Detailed procedures, licences and schedules under the 1940 Act |
| 1948 | Pharmacy Act | Regulation of the pharmacy profession; PCI set up in 1949 |
| 1954 | Drugs and Magic Remedies (Objectionable Advertisements) Act | Stops misleading drug advertisements |
| 1955 | Essential Commodities Act | Basis for drug price control orders |
| 1960 | Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act | Controls experiments on animals |
| 1970 | Patents Act | Patent law; product patents for medicines came back in 2005 |
| 1970 onwards | Drugs (Prices Control) Orders (1970, 1979, 1987, 1995, 2013) | Control of medicine prices |
| 1971 | Medical Termination of Pregnancy Act | Safe and legal abortion; amended in 2021 |
| 1985 | Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act | Replaced the Opium Acts and the Dangerous Drugs Act |
| 1986 | Environment (Protection) Act | Parent Act for the Bio-Medical Waste Management Rules, 2016 |
| 1997 | National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority set up | Fixes and enforces drug prices |
| 2005 | Disaster Management Act | National, state and district disaster authorities |
| 2006 | Food Safety and Standards Act | Food and food supplements; FSSAI |
| 2010 | Clinical Establishments (Registration and Regulation) Act | Registration and minimum standards of hospitals and clinics |
| 2015 | Pharmacy Practice Regulations | Duties and ethics of registered pharmacists |
| 2017 | Medical Devices Rules | Separate rules for medical devices under the 1940 Act |
| 2019 | New Drugs and Clinical Trials Rules; Consumer Protection Act | New drug approval and trials; new consumer law |
| 2020 | Education Regulations (ER-2020) | Present D.Pharm course |

### Other important committees

- **Hathi Committee (Committee on Drugs and Pharmaceutical Industry), 1974–75** – recommended a list of essential drugs, use of generic names and a larger role for Indian companies.
- These ideas later appeared in the **National List of Essential Medicines** and in pricing policies (Unit 7).

## 1.7 Acts covered in this subject

```text
Profession          -> Pharmacy Act 1948, Pharmacy Practice Regulations 2015, Code of Ethics
Quality of drugs    -> Drugs and Cosmetics Act 1940 + Rules 1945, Medical Devices Rules 2017,
                       New Drugs and Clinical Trials Rules 2019
Misuse and poisons  -> NDPS Act 1985, Poisons Act 1919
Advertising         -> Drugs and Magic Remedies Act 1954
Prices              -> DPCO 2013, Pharmaceutical Policy 2002, NLEM
Animals and humans  -> Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act 1960, ICMR guidelines, bioethics
Health services     -> MTP Act, Clinical Establishments Act, blood bank rules, BMW Rules 2016
Food supplements    -> Food Safety and Standards Act 2006
Citizens            -> Consumer Protection Act 2019, Disaster Management Act 2005
Innovation          -> Patents Act 1970, intellectual property rights
```

## 1.8 Why a pharmacist must know the law

1. Only a **registered pharmacist** may dispense medicines; registration itself is a legal status.
2. Every pharmacy works under a **drug licence** with conditions that must be followed.
3. The pharmacist decides which medicines need a prescription and which records to keep.
4. Breaking these rules can lead to cancellation of the licence, removal from the register, fine or imprisonment.
5. The law protects the patient; knowing it helps the pharmacist protect the public.

## Remember

- Drugs and poisons, and the medical and other professions, are in the **Concurrent List**: both Parliament and States can make laws.
- An **Act** gives the main law; **Rules** give the detailed procedure; **Regulations** are made by statutory bodies; **Schedules** are lists that can be changed by notification.
- A Bill becomes an Act after passing both Houses and receiving the **President's assent**.
- **Chopra Committee (1930–31)** → Drugs Act 1940 and Pharmacy Act 1948.
- The **NDPS Act, 1985** replaced the Opium Acts and the Dangerous Drugs Act, 1930.
- Laws change often: always check the latest amendment and notification.

# Unit 2: Pharmacy Act, 1948 and Pharmacy Practice Regulations, 2015

This unit covers syllabus chapter 2: the Act that created the Pharmacy Council of India and the State Pharmacy Councils, education regulations, registration of pharmacists, offences, and the Pharmacy Practice Regulations, 2015. It is one of the most frequently examined chapters.

## 2.1 Objectives of the Pharmacy Act, 1948

The Act was passed on the advice of the Chopra Committee. Its main aims are:

1. To **regulate the profession and practice of pharmacy** in India.
2. To make sure that only **properly qualified persons** practise as pharmacists.
3. To set up the **Pharmacy Council of India (PCI)** to lay down **uniform minimum standards of pharmacy education**.
4. To set up **State Pharmacy Councils** (and Joint State Councils) to **register pharmacists** and keep their registers.
5. To punish unqualified persons who dispense medicines or falsely claim to be registered.

The PCI was constituted in **1949**. The Act extends to the whole of India.

### Chapters of the Act

| Chapter | Contents |
| --- | --- |
| I | Short title, extent, definitions |
| II | Pharmacy Council of India: constitution, officers, education regulations, approval of courses and institutions |
| III | State Pharmacy Councils and Joint State Pharmacy Councils |
| IV | Registration of pharmacists, removal and restoration |
| V | Miscellaneous: inspectors, offences and penalties, power to make rules |

## 2.2 Important definitions

| Term | Meaning (in simple words) |
| --- | --- |
| Central Council | The Pharmacy Council of India |
| State Council | A State Pharmacy Council set up under the Act (includes a Joint State Council where one exists) |
| Joint State Council | One council formed by agreement between two or more States |
| Register | The register of pharmacists kept by a State Council |
| Registered pharmacist | A person whose name is entered in the register of a State for the time being |
| Central Register | The all-India register of pharmacists kept by the PCI |
| Agreement | An agreement between States to form a Joint State Council |

## 2.3 Pharmacy Council of India

### Constitution (who the members are)

The PCI has three kinds of members: **elected**, **nominated** and **ex officio**.

| Type | Members |
| --- | --- |
| Elected by the University Grants Commission | Six teachers of pharmacy colleges, with at least one teacher each of pharmaceutical chemistry, pharmaceutics (pharmacy), pharmacology and pharmacognosy |
| Nominated by the Central Government | Six members, of whom at least four hold a degree or diploma in pharmacy or pharmaceutical chemistry and practise pharmacy |
| Elected by the medical council | One member (the Act names the Medical Council of India, which was replaced by the National Medical Commission in 2020) |
| Ex officio | Director General of Health Services; Drugs Controller (General) of India; Director of the Central Drugs Laboratory |
| Nominated by UGC and AICTE | One representative each |
| Elected by each State Council | One registered pharmacist from each State |
| Nominated by each State Government | One registered pharmacist from each State |

- The members elect a **President** and a **Vice-President** from among themselves.
- Elected and nominated members hold office for **five years** and may be re-elected or re-nominated.
- The Council appoints a **Registrar** (who acts as secretary) and other staff.
- An **Executive Committee** (President, Vice-President and some members) handles day-to-day work.

### Functions of the PCI

1. **Education Regulations** – prescribes the minimum standard of education for registration as a pharmacist: course of study, duration, practical training, subjects, examinations, staff, equipment and accommodation of institutions.
2. **Approval of courses and institutions** – an authority conducting a course may apply for approval; the Council approves it if it meets the regulations. Only an approved qualification leads to registration.
3. **Withdrawal of approval** – if an institution stops meeting the standards, the Council can withdraw approval after giving it a chance to explain (with the Central Government's role as the Act provides).
4. **Inspection** – appoints inspectors to inspect institutions and examinations, and reports to the Council.
5. **Qualifications from outside India** – decides whether foreign pharmacy qualifications can be accepted.
6. **Central Register of Pharmacists** – keeps an all-India register based on the State registers.
7. Advises the Central and State Governments on pharmacy education and practice; frames regulations such as the **Pharmacy Practice Regulations, 2015**.

## 2.4 Education Regulations

Under the Act the PCI has framed several Education Regulations for the diploma; the present one is **Education Regulations 2020 (ER-2020)**.

| Feature | ER-2020 (D.Pharm) |
| --- | --- |
| Entry qualification | 10+2 with physics, chemistry and biology or mathematics (as the regulations lay down) |
| Duration | Two academic years |
| Practical training | Not less than 500 hours, spread over at least three months, in a hospital or community pharmacy approved under the regulations |
| Subjects | Pharmaceutics, pharmaceutical chemistry, pharmacognosy, human anatomy and physiology, social pharmacy (first year); pharmacology, community pharmacy and management, biochemistry and clinical pathology, pharmacotherapeutics, hospital and clinical pharmacy, pharmacy law and ethics (second year) |
| Examinations | Yearly; theory and practical with sessional marks |
| Exit examination | PCI has notified a D.Pharm exit examination before registration; check its current status and dates |

The regulations also set staff qualifications, laboratory equipment, library and building requirements for an institution.

## 2.5 State Pharmacy Councils and Joint State Councils

### Constitution of a State Pharmacy Council

| Type | Members |
| --- | --- |
| Elected | Six registered pharmacists, elected by registered pharmacists of the State |
| Nominated by the State Government | Five members, of whom at least three hold a degree or diploma in pharmacy or pharmaceutical chemistry, or are registered pharmacists |
| Elected by the State Medical Council | One member |
| Ex officio | Chief administrative medical officer of the State; officer in charge of drugs control in the State; Government Analyst under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act (or as the Act names) |

- Members elect a **President** and **Vice-President**; term is **five years**.
- The Council appoints a **Registrar**, who keeps the register of pharmacists.

### Functions of a State Council

1. Prepare and maintain the **register of pharmacists** of the State.
2. Register qualified persons and issue certificates of registration.
3. Renew registrations and keep the register up to date.
4. Remove names for misconduct or other reasons, and restore names when justified.
5. Appoint **pharmacy inspectors** to inspect premises where drugs are compounded or dispensed.
6. Send copies of the register to the PCI.

### Joint State Pharmacy Council

Two or more States (or a State and a Union Territory) may make an **agreement** to form one Joint Council for all of them, for a fixed period that can be renewed. Its constitution is similar to a State Council, with members from each State in the agreement.

## 2.6 Registration of pharmacists

### Who can be registered

A person may apply for registration in a State if he or she:

1. Has reached the age set by the Act (18 years);
2. Resides or carries on business or profession of pharmacy in that State; and
3. Holds an **approved qualification** (D.Pharm or higher) and meets the conditions of the Education Regulations, including practical training (and the exit examination where it applies).

The first registers (when the Act started) also allowed persons with a fixed number of years of practical experience in compounding to be registered. That was a one-time provision.

### Steps

```text
Application to Registrar of State Council (with fee, documents)
          |
          v
Registrar checks qualification -> name entered in register
          |
          v
Certificate of registration issued -> renewal at intervals with fee
          |
          v
Name sent to PCI for the Central Register
```

### Removal from the register

The Executive Committee of a State Council may remove a name if the pharmacist:

- has been convicted of an offence that the Council considers involves moral turpitude or makes the person unfit to practise;
- has been found guilty of **infamous conduct** in a professional respect (professional misconduct) after an inquiry; or
- has got registration by fraud or by mistake; or fails to pay the renewal fee.

The person is given a chance to be heard. An **appeal** lies to the State Government within the period set by the Act. A name may be **restored** later if the Council is satisfied.

## 2.7 Offences and penalties

| Offence | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| Falsely claiming to be registered | Using the title "registered pharmacist" or similar words when not registered |
| Dispensing by an unregistered person | Compounding, preparing, mixing or dispensing any medicine on a medical practitioner's prescription by anyone other than a registered pharmacist (a medical practitioner may supply medicines to his own patients) |
| Failure to surrender the certificate | Not returning the certificate after removal from the register |
| Obstructing an inspector | Refusing entry or information to a pharmacy inspector |
| Employing unregistered persons | Employer allowing dispensing by an unregistered person is also punishable |

Punishment is a **fine, imprisonment, or both**, with heavier punishment for repeat offences. The amounts set in the 1948 Act have been changed by amendments, so **check the current Act for the exact figures**.

## 2.8 Pharmacy Practice Regulations, 2015

The PCI framed these regulations in **2015** under the Pharmacy Act. They lay down how a registered pharmacist must practise.

### Main points

1. **Definitions** – pharmacist, pharmacy practice, patient counselling, professional misconduct and so on.
2. **Duties of a pharmacist** – dispense only against a valid prescription where the law requires one; check the prescription for errors and interactions; counsel the patient on dose, use, storage and side-effects; keep records; maintain confidentiality.
3. **Display** – the registration certificate should be displayed in the pharmacy; the pharmacist should be identifiable (name badge, apron) as the regulations require.
4. **Patient medication records** and dispensing records to be kept for the period laid down.
5. **Continuing education** – pharmacists are expected to update their knowledge through continuing pharmacy education programmes.
6. **Code of ethics** – duties towards patients, prescribers, the public and the profession (detailed in Unit 8).
7. **Professional misconduct** – for example: allowing an unregistered person to dispense; dispensing a prescription-only medicine without prescription; substituting without consent; selling spurious or expired medicines; giving false certificates; advertising in an undignified way; accepting gifts or commissions to promote particular products; breaching confidentiality.
8. **Punishment** – a State Council may warn, suspend registration for a period, or remove the name, after an inquiry.

### Pharmacist roles named in the regulations

| Setting | Role |
| --- | --- |
| Community pharmacy | Dispensing, counselling, OTC advice, health promotion |
| Hospital pharmacy | Procurement, storage, inpatient and outpatient dispensing, drug information |
| Clinical pharmacy | Medication review, adverse drug reaction monitoring, rational use |
| Other | Drug information centres, public health programmes |

## Remember

- Pharmacy Act **1948**; PCI constituted **1949**; aim: regulate the profession and set **minimum standards of education**.
- PCI has **elected, nominated and ex officio** members; term **five years**; President and Vice-President elected by members.
- PCI frames **Education Regulations** (now ER-2020), approves courses and institutions, can withdraw approval, keeps the **Central Register**.
- State Councils keep the **register of pharmacists**, appoint pharmacy inspectors, remove names for misconduct (appeal to State Government).
- Only a **registered pharmacist** may dispense on prescription; claiming falsely to be registered is an offence.
- **Pharmacy Practice Regulations, 2015**: duties, records, counselling, professional misconduct and punishment.

# Unit 3: Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 and Rules, 1945 – I (objectives, definitions, schedules, import, administration)

Syllabus chapter 3 is the biggest chapter in this subject (23 of 75 hours). In this guide it is split into two units. This unit covers the objectives, legal definitions, the list of schedules, import of drugs and the authorities that run the Act. Unit 4 covers manufacture, the important schedules in detail, sale, records and banned drugs.

## 3.1 Objectives of the Act

The Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 (with the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, 1945 made under it) aims to:

1. Regulate the **import, manufacture, distribution and sale** of drugs and cosmetics in India.
2. Make sure that drugs sold are **safe, effective and of standard quality**, and that cosmetics are safe.
3. Prevent the sale of **misbranded, adulterated and spurious** drugs and cosmetics.
4. Regulate the **manufacture of Ayurvedic, Siddha and Unani (ASU)** drugs for sale.
5. Set up **advisory and testing bodies** (DTAB, DCC, CDL) and appoint **analysts and inspectors** to enforce the law.

The Act was first passed as the Drugs Act, 1940; it was later amended to cover cosmetics and renamed. It has been amended many times (for example, the 2008 amendment made punishments for spurious drugs much heavier). Medical devices are now regulated under the **Medical Devices Rules, 2017** made under this same Act (Unit 10), and new drugs and clinical trials under the **New Drugs and Clinical Trials Rules, 2019** (Unit 11).

## 3.2 Important definitions

### Drug

"Drug" is defined very widely. It includes:

1. All **medicines for internal or external use** of human beings or animals, and all substances used for the diagnosis, treatment, mitigation or prevention of any disease or disorder, including preparations applied to the body to repel insects such as mosquitoes;
2. Substances (other than food) intended to **affect the structure or any function** of the human body, or to destroy vermin or insects that cause disease;
3. Substances intended to be used as **components of a drug**, including empty gelatin capsules; and
4. **Devices** notified by the Central Government after consulting the DTAB (this is how medical devices came under the Act).

### Cosmetic

Any article meant to be **rubbed, poured, sprinkled or sprayed on, introduced into, or otherwise applied to the human body** for **cleansing, beautifying, promoting attractiveness or altering the appearance**, including any article meant to be a component of a cosmetic. **Soap is excluded.**

### Misbranded drug

A drug is misbranded if:

- it is coloured, coated, powdered or polished so that damage is hidden, or it is made to appear of better value than it is;
- it is **not labelled** in the prescribed manner; or
- its label or container carries any **false or misleading statement or claim**.

### Adulterated drug

A drug is adulterated if:

- it contains any **filthy, putrid or decomposed** substance;
- it was prepared, packed or stored under **insanitary conditions** where it may have become contaminated;
- its container is made of a **poisonous or harmful** substance that may make the contents harmful;
- it contains a **colour other than one prescribed**;
- it contains any **harmful or toxic** substance; or
- any substance has been **mixed** with it so as to reduce its quality or strength.

### Spurious drug

A drug is spurious if:

- it is imported or made under a **name that belongs to another drug**;
- it is an **imitation of, or a substitute for, another drug** or resembles it so as to deceive, or carries the name of another drug;
- its label carries the name of a manufacturer that is **fictitious or does not exist**;
- it has been **substituted** wholly or partly by another drug or substance; or
- it claims to be the product of a manufacturer who did not actually make it.

| Type | Key idea | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Misbranded | Wrong or misleading label or appearance | Tablet label without batch number or with a false claim |
| Adulterated | Quality spoiled by contamination or mixing | Syrup made in dirty conditions, containing fungus |
| Spurious | Fake identity | Chalk tablets sold in a famous brand's packing |
| Not of standard quality | Fails the official standard | Tablet with 80% of the labelled content |

Similar definitions exist for **misbranded, adulterated and spurious cosmetics**.

### Other definitions

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Manufacture | Any process of making, altering, ornamenting, finishing, packing, labelling, breaking up or otherwise treating a drug or cosmetic with a view to its sale or distribution. Compounding or dispensing in the ordinary course of retail business is **not** manufacture |
| Patent or proprietary medicine | (for modern medicine) a drug presented in a form ready for use whose formula is not in the Indian Pharmacopoeia or another recognised pharmacopoeia; (for ASU) a ready-to-use drug whose formula is not in the authoritative ASU books |
| Ayurvedic, Siddha or Unani drug | A drug made exclusively according to the formulae in the authoritative books listed in the First Schedule |
| Government Analyst | An analyst appointed by the Central or State Government under the Act |
| Inspector | A drug inspector appointed under the Act |
| Standard quality | A drug that complies with the standards in the Second Schedule to the Act |

## 3.3 Schedules to the Act and to the Rules

### Schedules to the Act

| Schedule | Contents |
| --- | --- |
| First Schedule | List of authoritative books of Ayurveda, Siddha and Unani systems |
| Second Schedule | Standards to be complied with by imported drugs and by drugs made for sale (for example, the Indian Pharmacopoeia for drugs in it) |

### Schedules to the Rules (short legal meaning of each)

| Schedule | What it lays down |
| --- | --- |
| A | Forms (applications, licences, reports) |
| B | Fees for test or analysis by the Central Drugs Laboratory or State laboratories |
| C | Biological and special products (sera, vaccines, toxins, antigens, insulin, sterile parenteral preparations and similar) – special licence and care |
| C(1) | Other special products (for example, digitalis and ergot preparations, some antibiotics and vitamins not for injection) |
| D | Classes of drugs exempted from certain import provisions |
| E(1) | Poisonous substances under the ASU systems |
| F, F(1), F(2), F(3), FF | Requirements for blood banks and blood products, vaccines and sera, surgical dressings, umbilical tapes, ophthalmic preparations |
| G | Drugs to be used under medical supervision – caution label |
| H | Prescription drugs – sold by retail only on a doctor's prescription |
| H1 | Specified antibiotics, anti-TB drugs and habit-forming drugs – prescription plus a separate register |
| J | Diseases and ailments that no drug may claim to prevent or cure |
| K | Drugs exempted from certain provisions (for example, household remedies sold in villages) |
| M | Good Manufacturing Practices and requirements of premises, plant and equipment |
| M-I, M-II | GMP for homoeopathic medicines and for cosmetics |
| N | Minimum equipment and requirements for the efficient running of a pharmacy |
| O | Standards for disinfectant fluids |
| P | Life period (shelf life) and storage conditions of drugs |
| P1 | Pack sizes of drugs |
| Q | Coal tar colours and dyes allowed in cosmetics |
| R | Standards for condoms and other mechanical contraceptives |
| S | Standards for cosmetics |
| T | GMP for Ayurvedic, Siddha and Unani drugs |
| U, U(1) | Particulars to be shown in manufacturing and analytical records of drugs and of cosmetics |
| V | Standards for patent or proprietary medicines |
| X | Narcotic and psychotropic drugs that need special licences, prescriptions and records |
| Y | Requirements for clinical trials – now replaced by the New Drugs and Clinical Trials Rules, 2019 |

Schedules are changed by notification, so check the latest version. A revised **Schedule M** (GMP) was notified at the end of 2023, with later deadlines for small units to comply; check the current dates.

## 3.4 Import of drugs

### Classes of drugs and cosmetics prohibited from import

No person may import:

1. Drugs or cosmetics that are **not of standard quality**.
2. **Misbranded, adulterated or spurious** drugs, and misbranded or spurious cosmetics.
3. Drugs or cosmetics whose import has been **prohibited by notification** (for example, drugs not in the public interest or banned in the country of origin as the rules say).
4. Any drug that claims to **cure or prevent any disease listed in Schedule J**, or any other disease the Government notifies.
5. **Patent or proprietary medicines** that do not show the true formula or list of active ingredients and their quantities on the label.
6. Any drug or cosmetic that is **not labelled** as the rules require.
7. Cosmetics containing harmful ingredients that the Government has prohibited, and cosmetics tested on animals where the rules forbid such import.
8. Drugs imported without a **licence** where a licence is required.

### Import under licence or permit

```text
Foreign manufacturer and its products
        |  Registration certificate (Form 41) from the Central licensing authority (DCGI)
        v
Indian importer
        |  Import licence: Form 10 (drugs other than Schedule X)
        |                  Form 10A (Schedule X drugs)
        v
Imported through notified ports, checked by CDSCO port officers and customs
```

| Purpose | Permission |
| --- | --- |
| Commercial import | Registration certificate for the foreign site and products, plus an import licence (Form 10 / 10A) |
| Import for examination, test or analysis | A test licence (Form 11), for small quantities, not for sale |
| Import for personal use | Small quantities for the importer's own treatment are allowed under the rules, with a permit where required |
| Import of a new drug | Permission under the New Drugs and Clinical Trials Rules, 2019 |
| Import of medical devices | Licence under the Medical Devices Rules, 2017 |

Applications are now made online through the **SUGAM portal** of CDSCO. Form numbers and fees are revised from time to time; **check the current rules** before applying.

Conditions of an import licence include: storage under proper conditions, keeping records of import and sale, allowing inspection, testing samples if asked, and labelling with the importer's name and licence number.

## 3.5 Administration of the Act and Rules

```text
                   Central Government (Ministry of Health)
                    |               |                |
                 DTAB             DCC             CDL, Kolkata
          (technical advice)  (uniform working)  (appellate testing)
                    |
      CDSCO headed by Drugs Controller General of India
      (central licensing: imports, new drugs, Schedule C/C1 and blood products, devices)
                    |
           State Drugs Control Departments
      (licensing authorities, controlling authority, drug inspectors,
       State drug-testing laboratories with Government Analysts)
```

### Drugs Technical Advisory Board (DTAB)

- **Function:** advises the Central and State Governments on **technical matters** arising from the Act, and carries out other functions given to it.
- **Members:** ex officio members such as the **Director General of Health Services (Chairman)**, the Drugs Controller General of India, the Director of the Central Drugs Laboratory, the heads of national research institutes (for example, the Central Research Institute, Kasauli and the Indian Veterinary Research Institute), and the Presidents of the pharmacy and medical councils; plus nominated and elected members, including State drug control officers, pharmacy and medicine teachers, an industry representative and Government Analysts.
- Nominated and elected members hold office for **three years**.
- The DTAB is consulted before schedules are changed or a drug is banned.

### Central Drugs Laboratory (CDL), Kolkata

- Tests samples of drugs and cosmetics sent by **customs officers** (imports) and by **courts**.
- Acts as the **appellate laboratory**: when a party disputes a State Government Analyst's report, the court can send a sample to CDL, and its report is conclusive.
- Other central laboratories do the same work for particular products (for example, CRI Kasauli for vaccines and sera).

### Drugs Consultative Committee (DCC)

- **Members:** two representatives of the Central Government and **one representative of each State Government**.
- **Function:** advises the Central and State Governments and the DTAB on matters needed to secure **uniform administration of the Act across India**.
- It meets when the Central Government calls it and decides its own procedure.

### Government Analysts

- Appointed by the Central or State Government with qualifications set by the rules.
- They test samples sent by inspectors (or by others under the Act) and give a **report in the prescribed form**, stating whether the sample is of standard quality.
- Their report is evidence in court; the accused can challenge it, and the sample can then go to CDL.

### Licensing authorities

| Authority | Licences issued |
| --- | --- |
| Central Licensing Authority (DCGI) | Import, new drugs and clinical trials; approval of licences for Schedule C/C(1) products such as vaccines, sera, blood products, large volume parenterals and some biologicals; class C and D medical devices |
| State Licensing Authority | Manufacture licences for most drugs and cosmetics; all sale licences (retail and wholesale); class A and B medical devices |

### Controlling authority

The officer appointed by the State Government to control the licensing authority's work and the drug inspectors; in most States this is the **Drugs Controller** of the State.

### Drug Inspectors

**Qualifications:** a degree in pharmacy, pharmaceutical sciences or medicine (with the specialisations and experience the rules prescribe); for some inspections (for example, of biologicals) further experience is required.

**Powers** (within the area assigned):

1. Inspect any premises where drugs or cosmetics are made, stored, sold or distributed, and the materials and records there.
2. **Take samples** (paying the price and giving a receipt; sample divided into portions – one sent to the Government Analyst, one given to the person, others kept).
3. Search any place, person or vehicle where he has reason to believe an offence is being committed.
4. **Stop and seize** drugs, cosmetics, records and materials that he believes break the Act, and order that stock not be disposed of.
5. Examine records and registers, and require production of documents.

**Duties:** inspect licensed premises regularly as the rules require, check that licence conditions are followed, investigate complaints, send samples for testing, start prosecutions with the authority's sanction, and report to the controlling authority. An inspector must not disclose information obtained except in the course of duty.

## 3.6 Penalties (overview)

The Act provides graded punishments. The heaviest are for manufacturing or selling **spurious or adulterated drugs**: where such a drug is likely to cause death or grievous hurt, the 2008 amendment provides imprisonment of **not less than ten years, which may extend to life**, and a heavy fine. Lesser offences (not-of-standard-quality drugs, selling without a licence, failure to keep records) carry shorter imprisonment and fines. Special courts may try offences relating to spurious and adulterated drugs. Because amounts are revised, **check the current Act for exact figures**.

## Remember

- Objective: control **import, manufacture, distribution and sale** so that drugs are of standard quality.
- "Drug" includes components (empty capsules) and **notified devices**; "cosmetic" excludes **soap**.
- **Misbranded** = wrong label/appearance; **adulterated** = contaminated/mixed; **spurious** = fake identity.
- First Schedule = ASU books; Second Schedule = standards; Schedule **Y** replaced by NDCT Rules, 2019.
- Import licences: **Form 10** (non-X), **Form 10A** (Schedule X), registration certificate **Form 41**, test licence **Form 11**.
- **DTAB** = technical advice; **DCC** = uniform administration; **CDL Kolkata** = appellate laboratory.
- Drug inspectors can **inspect, sample, search and seize**.

# Unit 4: Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 and Rules, 1945 – II (manufacture, schedules, sale, records, banned drugs)

This unit continues syllabus chapter 3. It covers licences for manufacture, the schedules named in the syllabus (C and C1, G, H, H1, K, P, M, N and X), licences for sale, the records a pharmacy must keep, and drugs banned in India. Examiners love tables of licence forms and schedule labels, so learn them well.

## 4.1 Manufacture of drugs

### Prohibition of manufacture and sale of certain drugs

No person may manufacture for sale, sell, stock, exhibit or distribute:

1. Any drug that is **not of standard quality**, or is **misbranded, adulterated or spurious**.
2. Any **patent or proprietary medicine** whose label does not show the true formula or list of active ingredients with quantities.
3. Any drug that claims to **prevent or cure a disease in Schedule J**.
4. Any drug made in breach of the Act or its Rules, or **without a licence**.
5. Any drug whose manufacture or sale has been **prohibited by the Central Government** (section 26A, see 4.6).

### Types of manufacturing licence

| Licence | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| Form 25 | Manufacture for sale of drugs **other than** those in Schedules C, C(1) and X |
| Form 28 | Manufacture for sale of drugs in **Schedules C and C(1)** (excluding Schedule X) |
| Form 25A | **Loan licence** for drugs other than C, C(1) and X |
| Form 28A | **Loan licence** for drugs in Schedules C and C(1) |
| Form 25B | **Repacking** licence (drugs other than C, C(1) and X) |
| Form 29 | Licence to manufacture drugs for **examination, test or analysis** |
| Separate forms | Manufacture of Schedule X drugs, cosmetics, homoeopathic medicines and ASU drugs each have their own licences |

The State licensing authority grants most licences. For Schedule C/C(1) products such as vaccines, sera, blood products and large volume parenterals, the licence needs the approval of the **Central Licence Approving Authority (DCGI)**. Form numbers are revised from time to time, so confirm with the current rules.

### Conditions for grant of a manufacturing licence

1. **Premises, plant and equipment** that meet **Schedule M** (GMP).
2. **Competent technical staff**: manufacture under the active direction of a person with a degree in pharmacy, pharmaceutical chemistry or chemistry (or as the rules list) with practical experience.
3. A **testing unit** of its own with a competent analytical chemist, or arrangement with an approved laboratory where the rules allow.
4. Proper storage facilities for raw materials and finished products.
5. Inspection of the premises by drug inspectors before grant.

### Conditions of a manufacturing licence (after grant)

1. Keep **manufacturing and analytical records** as given in **Schedule U**, for the period prescribed.
2. Test every batch of raw material and finished product before release.
3. Allow inspectors to enter, inspect and take samples at any time.
4. Supply samples to the authority when asked.
5. Report changes in technical staff or premises.
6. Comply with Schedule M continuously; recall defective batches.
7. Pay the licence or **retention fee** on time. Under the present rules most licences no longer expire after a fixed period but remain valid while the retention fee is paid at the set interval; check the current rule.

### Manufacture for examination, test or analysis

A small quantity of a drug may be made for **test, examination or analysis** (for example, for stability studies or to develop a product) under a test licence (Form 29). The quantity is limited, the drug cannot be sold, and records of making, use and disposal must be kept.

### Manufacture of a new drug

A **new drug** (not yet approved in India, or a new indication, dosage form, route or combination of an approved drug) can be manufactured for sale only after permission from the **Central Licensing Authority** under the **New Drugs and Clinical Trials Rules, 2019** (Unit 11). After that, the State licence is endorsed for the product.

### Loan licence

A **loan licence** is given to a person (the loan licensee) who **does not own** a manufacturing unit but uses the premises, equipment and technical staff of another licensed manufacturer to make his products. Both are responsible for quality. It allows small marketing companies to get products made without building a factory.

### Repacking licence

**Repacking** means breaking up a drug from a bulk container into smaller packs for sale or distribution (for example, repacking a bulk powder or tablets into small packs). It needs a separate licence (Form 25B), suitable premises and a competent person, and repackers must label packs correctly and keep records. Some products (for example, Schedule C/C(1) items) may not be repacked under this licence.

## 4.2 Schedules named in the syllabus

| Schedule | What it covers | Examples | Label / special rule |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **C** | Biological and special products, mostly parenteral | Vaccines, sera, toxoids, antigens, insulin, heparin, sterile injections | Form 28 licence; cold storage and special testing |
| **C(1)** | Other special products, mostly non-parenteral | Digitalis and ergot preparations, some antibiotics and vitamins for oral use, ophthalmic preparations | Form 28 licence; storage as labelled |
| **G** | Drugs that should be taken under medical supervision | Several antihistamines and oral antidiabetics, as listed | Label: **"Caution: It is dangerous to take this preparation except under medical supervision"** |
| **H** | Prescription drugs | Most antibiotics, antihypertensives, steroids, as listed | Symbol **Rx** and warning: **"Schedule H drug – Warning: To be sold by retail on the prescription of a Registered Medical Practitioner only"** |
| **H1** | Specified 3rd/4th generation antibiotics, anti-TB drugs and habit-forming drugs (added in 2013) | Cefepime, meropenem, moxifloxacin, isoniazid, rifampicin, ethambutol, pyrazinamide, alprazolam, zolpidem, buprenorphine | **Rx** in red and a warning in a box with a red border: dangerous to take except on medical advice, not to be sold without prescription. Separate **H1 register** |
| **K** | Exemptions from certain provisions | Household remedies (for example, simple pain relievers, antacids, balms as listed) sold by shops in villages; drugs supplied by a doctor to his own patients; drugs supplied by hospitals to their patients | Conditions in the schedule must be met |
| **P** | Life period (expiry) of drugs and storage conditions | Shelf life of listed drugs, such as antibiotics | Expiry not to exceed the stated period unless approved |
| **M** | Good Manufacturing Practices | Premises, sanitation, staff, equipment, documentation, quality control | Must be followed by every drug factory |
| **N** | Minimum equipment of a pharmacy | Premises, dispensing equipment, reference books | Must be followed by pharmacies that compound and dispense |
| **X** | Narcotic and psychotropic drugs with high misuse potential | Amphetamine, methylphenidate, barbiturates such as amobarbital, pentobarbital and secobarbital | **XRx** in red and warning; special licences, prescriptions in duplicate, separate records, locked storage |

### Schedule H1 in detail

- Introduced to control **misuse of antibiotics (to slow antimicrobial resistance)** and of habit-forming drugs.
- The retailer must record in a **separate register**: name and address of the prescriber, name of the patient, name of the drug and quantity supplied.
- The register must be kept for **three years** and be open to inspection.

### Schedule X in detail

- Needs **special licences** for manufacture and sale (retail and wholesale).
- Prescription must be in **duplicate**; the retailer keeps one copy for the period laid down (two years).
- Drugs must be kept under **lock and key** in a separate place.
- Records of purchase and sale are kept separately and checked by inspectors.
- Manufacturers must report stock and sales to the authorities as the rules require.

### Schedule M (GMP) in brief

```text
Premises      -> location away from pollution, proper drains, separate areas for
                 raw materials, production, packing, quarantine, finished goods
Personnel     -> qualified and trained staff, health checks, hygiene, clean clothing
Equipment     -> suitable, cleaned, calibrated, maintained, with logs
Materials     -> tested, quarantined, labelled, stored properly
Production    -> written procedures, batch records, line clearance, in-process checks
Quality control -> independent QC department; testing, stability, retained samples
Documentation -> master formula, batch records, SOPs, distribution and complaint records
Other         -> self-inspection, recall procedure, validation, complaints handling
```

### Schedule N in brief

- **Premises:** a pharmacy should be clean, separated from living quarters, with proper light and ventilation, and with the area the rules require.
- **Equipment:** prescription balance and weights, measures, mortars and pestles, spatulas, funnels, glass and porcelain vessels, refrigerator, water bath, hot plate, ointment slab, and other dispensing items listed.
- **Books:** the current Indian Pharmacopoeia and the National Formulary of India, and other standard references.
- **Staff:** a registered pharmacist in charge of compounding and dispensing.

## 4.3 Sale of drugs

### Types of sale licence

| Licence | Who it is for |
| --- | --- |
| **Form 20** | Retail sale of drugs other than those in Schedules C, C(1) and X |
| **Form 21** | Retail sale of drugs in Schedules C and C(1), excluding X |
| **Form 20B** | Wholesale of drugs other than C, C(1) and X |
| **Form 21B** | Wholesale of drugs in Schedules C and C(1) |
| **Form 20F / 20G** | Retail / wholesale of Schedule X drugs |
| **Form 20A / 21A** | **Restricted licences** for dealers who do not employ a pharmacist (for example, general stores in villages or itinerant vendors), for selling only certain drugs in sealed packs |

Licences are issued by the **State licensing authority**. Form numbers and fees are revised from time to time; check the current rules.

### Conditions for a retail sale licence

1. **Premises** of adequate area (the rules prescribe a minimum floor area), clean and well lit, with proper storage.
2. A **refrigerator** where drugs need cold storage.
3. Sale under the **personal supervision of a registered pharmacist**.
4. Prescription drugs (H, H1, X) sold **only on a prescription** of a registered medical practitioner.
5. Drugs stored as labelled; expired drugs kept separately and not sold.
6. Licence displayed prominently.

### Conditions for a wholesale licence

1. Adequate premises and storage, including cold storage where needed.
2. Business under the charge of a **competent person** – a registered pharmacist, or a person with the educational qualification and experience in dealing with drugs that the rules prescribe.
3. Sale only to licensed retailers, hospitals, institutions and doctors, with proper invoices.

### Restricted licence

Given to a person who does not have a pharmacist (for example, a shop in a village where no pharmacy exists). It allows sale of **only certain drugs**, usually household remedies in **original sealed packs** from licensed manufacturers, without opening or compounding.

## 4.4 Records to be kept in a pharmacy

| Record | Details |
| --- | --- |
| Purchase records | Invoices with name of supplier, drug, batch number, quantity, expiry |
| Sale records (cash memo / bill) | For Schedule C, C(1), H, H1 and X drugs: name of patient and prescriber, drug, quantity, batch number |
| Prescription records | Prescriptions dispensed are stamped with the pharmacy's name and date to prevent reuse; prescription register for compounded medicines |
| **Schedule H1 register** | Prescriber, patient, drug and quantity; kept **three years** |
| **Schedule X records** | Duplicate prescription copy and separate register |
| NDPS records | For narcotic drugs, as the NDPS rules require (Unit 5) |
| Expiry and returns records | Expired or recalled stock, returned to supplier or destroyed properly |
| Temperature log | For refrigerated products such as vaccines and insulin |

Records must be kept for the periods the rules lay down and be shown to the inspector on demand.

## 4.5 Labelling of drugs (main points)

Labels of drugs for sale must show: name of the drug (generic name prominently), content of active ingredients, quantity, **batch number**, **manufacturing licence number**, **date of manufacture and expiry**, name and address of the manufacturer, storage conditions where needed, the schedule symbol and warning (Rx, XRx, caution), "for external use only" or "not for injection" where relevant, and the maximum retail price.

## 4.6 Drugs prohibited for manufacture and sale in India

- The Central Government can **prohibit** the manufacture, sale or distribution of any drug or cosmetic if it is satisfied, after consulting the DTAB, that the drug **involves risk to people or animals**, has **no therapeutic value claimed**, or has **no therapeutic justification** for its ingredients (section 26A).
- Many **irrational fixed-dose combinations (FDCs)** have been banned this way, for example a large group of FDCs banned in 2018.
- Examples of single drugs or uses banned in the past include **nimesulide formulations for children below 12 years**, **sibutramine** and **gatifloxacin** formulations for systemic use.
- A drug may also be restricted to certain uses instead of a full ban.
- The list changes often and some bans are challenged in court; **always check the current list on the CDSCO website**.

## Remember

- Manufacture licences: **25** (general), **28** (C and C1), **25A/28A** (loan), **25B** (repacking), **29** (test).
- Sale licences: **20/21** retail, **20B/21B** wholesale, **20F/20G** Schedule X, **20A/21A** restricted.
- Schedule **G** = caution label; **H** = Rx; **H1** = Rx in red + register for 3 years; **X** = XRx, duplicate prescription, lock and key.
- Schedule **M** = GMP; **N** = pharmacy equipment and books; **K** = exemptions; **P** = shelf life; **C/C1** = biologicals and special products.
- **Loan licence** = using another firm's factory; **repacking** = bulk to small packs.
- Section **26A** lets the Government ban drugs and irrational FDCs.

# Unit 5: Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985 and Poisons Act, 1919

This unit joins two short syllabus chapters (chapter 4, NDPS Act, and chapter 7, Poisons Act). Both laws control substances that are dangerous when misused. The NDPS Act is asked far more often.

## Part A: NDPS Act, 1985 and Rules

## 5.1 Background

Before 1985, narcotics were controlled by the **Opium Act, 1857**, the **Opium Act, 1878** and the **Dangerous Drugs Act, 1930**. These laws had light punishments and did not cover psychotropic substances. India had also signed three United Nations conventions:

| Convention | Subject |
| --- | --- |
| Single Convention on Narcotic Drugs, 1961 | Opium, coca, cannabis and their products |
| Convention on Psychotropic Substances, 1971 | Synthetic drugs that act on the mind (sedatives, stimulants, hallucinogens) |
| Convention against Illicit Traffic in Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances, 1988 | Drug trafficking, money from it, and precursor chemicals |

The **NDPS Act, 1985** replaced the old Acts and put India's obligations under these conventions into law. It has been amended several times (including in 1989, 2001 and 2014). The **NDPS Rules, 1985** (made by the Central Government) and State NDPS rules give the procedures.

## 5.2 Objectives

1. To **consolidate and amend** the law on narcotic drugs.
2. To make **stringent provisions** for the control and regulation of operations relating to narcotic drugs and psychotropic substances.
3. To provide for the **forfeiture of property** derived from illicit traffic.
4. To control **controlled substances** (precursor chemicals) used to make narcotics.
5. To carry out India's obligations under the **international conventions**.
6. To allow **medical and scientific use** while preventing misuse, and to provide for treatment of addicts.

## 5.3 Important definitions

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Addict | A person who has become dependent on any narcotic drug or psychotropic substance |
| Cannabis (hemp) | **Charas** (separated resin of the cannabis plant), **ganja** (flowering or fruiting tops, excluding seeds and leaves when not with the tops), and any mixture or drink made from them |
| Coca leaf | Leaf of the coca plant, except a leaf from which all alkaloids have been removed |
| Coca derivative | Crude cocaine, ecgonine and its derivatives, cocaine and its salts, and preparations containing more than the specified amount of cocaine |
| Opium | The coagulated juice of the opium poppy, and any mixture of it (with exceptions for preparations with very low morphine content) |
| Opium poppy | The plant *Papaver somniferum*, and any other plant species from which opium or its alkaloids can be extracted, as notified |
| Poppy straw | All parts of the opium poppy after harvesting (except seeds), whether in original form or cut or powdered |
| Manufactured drug | All coca derivatives, medicinal cannabis, opium derivatives and poppy straw concentrate, and any other narcotic substance the Government declares |
| Narcotic drug | Coca leaf, cannabis, opium, poppy straw and all manufactured drugs |
| Psychotropic substance | Any substance, natural or synthetic, or any salt or preparation of it, listed in the **Schedule to the Act** (for example, many barbiturates, benzodiazepines and amphetamines) |
| Controlled substance | A substance the Government declares controlled because it is used to make narcotic drugs or psychotropic substances (precursors such as acetic anhydride, ephedrine and pseudoephedrine) |
| Illicit traffic | Cultivating, producing, possessing, selling, buying, transporting, importing, exporting or financing any of these against the Act |
| Small quantity / commercial quantity | Quantities fixed by Government notification for each drug; punishment depends on them |
| Essential narcotic drugs | Narcotic drugs the Central Government notifies for medical and scientific use, regulated uniformly across India (introduced by the 2014 amendment to improve access to pain relief, for example morphine) |

## 5.4 Authorities and officers

| Level | Authority | Role |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Central | **Narcotics Commissioner** | Supervises cultivation of opium poppy and production of opium; issues licences for it |
| Central | **Narcotics Control Bureau (NCB)** | Coordinates enforcement against illicit traffic; works with States and international agencies |
| Central | **Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Consultative Committee** | Advises the Central Government on administration of the Act |
| Central | National Fund for Control of Drug Abuse | Money for fighting illicit traffic, treatment and rehabilitation of addicts |
| State | State Government and its officers (excise, police, drugs control) | Regulate possession, transport, sale and use within the State |
| Officers | Officers of central and state departments empowered by notification | Search, seizure and arrest under the Act |

## 5.5 Prohibition, control and regulation

### Prohibition

No person shall:

- **cultivate** any coca plant, or gather any part of it;
- **cultivate** the opium poppy or any cannabis plant; or
- **produce, manufacture, possess, sell, purchase, transport, warehouse, use, consume, import, export** or transship any narcotic drug or psychotropic substance,

**except for medical or scientific purposes** and in the manner and to the extent the Act, rules, licences and permits allow.

### Control by the Central Government

The Central Government regulates (through rules and licences):

1. Cultivation of the opium poppy and production of opium (in notified areas, by licensed cultivators).
2. **Manufacture of manufactured drugs** (for example, morphine, codeine) and psychotropic substances.
3. Import, export and transshipment of narcotics and psychotropics (import and export certificates).
4. Essential narcotic drugs (possession, transport, sale and use, uniformly in all States).
5. Controlled substances (precursors): manufacture, possession, sale, import and export.

### Control by State Governments

States regulate:

1. Possession, transport, purchase, sale and consumption of **poppy straw**, opium (where allowed), and **manufactured drugs** other than essential narcotic drugs.
2. Cultivation of cannabis for purposes other than ganja and charas, where allowed.
3. Licences to pharmacies, hospitals and practitioners to stock and dispense such drugs.

### What this means for a pharmacist

- A pharmacy needs the appropriate **licence or permit** to stock narcotic drugs (for example, codeine or morphine preparations).
- Sell only on a **valid prescription**; keep the drug locked; keep **records of receipt and issue** with the patient's and prescriber's details; report stocks as required; produce records to officers.
- Psychotropics such as benzodiazepines are also controlled under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act (Schedule H, H1 or X).

## 5.6 Offences and penalties

Punishment for most offences depends on the **quantity** involved:

| Quantity involved | Punishment (since the 2001 amendment) |
| --- | --- |
| **Small quantity** | Rigorous imprisonment up to **1 year**, or fine up to **₹10,000**, or both |
| More than small but less than commercial | Rigorous imprisonment up to **10 years** and fine up to **₹1 lakh** |
| **Commercial quantity** | Rigorous imprisonment of **not less than 10 years, up to 20 years**, and fine of **not less than ₹1 lakh, up to ₹2 lakh** (the court may impose more) |

Other important provisions:

- **Consumption** of a narcotic drug or psychotropic substance is itself an offence, with a lighter punishment, heavier for drugs like cocaine, morphine and heroin.
- **Repeat offenders** convicted again for large quantities face enhanced punishment; for certain very large quantities the court may impose the death penalty (made discretionary by the 2014 amendment).
- **Financing illicit traffic and harbouring offenders** are punished like the main offence.
- Offences relating to **controlled substances** (precursors) are punishable.
- **Property** derived from illicit traffic can be frozen and forfeited.
- Most offences are **cognizable and non-bailable**; special courts try them.
- **Addicts** who volunteer for treatment at a recognised centre can get immunity from prosecution for consumption and small-quantity possession, if conditions are met.
- Licensed persons who **contravene licence conditions** (for example, a pharmacy failing to keep records) are also punishable.

Since amounts and quantities are changed by notification and amendment, **check the current Act and notifications**.

## Part B: Poisons Act, 1919

## 5.7 Introduction and objective

The **Poisons Act, 1919** is a short, old Central Act. Its objective is to **regulate the import, possession and sale of poisons**. Most of the detail is in **rules made by each State Government**, so the actual list of poisons and conditions differs between States.

## 5.8 Definition

- **Poison** – any substance that the **State Government declares** to be a poison by notification for the purposes of the Act (for example, arsenic compounds, strychnine, cyanides, some pesticides, as listed in State rules).
- The Act does not apply to medicines dispensed in the normal way under other laws that already control them, as the rules provide.

## 5.9 Main provisions

### Possession of any poison

The State Government may make rules to **regulate the possession** of any specified poison in any local area, fixing the maximum quantity a person may possess without a licence.

### Possession for sale and sale of any poison

- Possession for sale and sale of any poison, by wholesale or retail, may be allowed **only under a licence** granted under State rules.
- State rules usually require the seller to:
  1. sell only to adults known to him or properly identified;
  2. enter every sale in a **poison register**: date, name and address of buyer, name and quantity of poison, purpose of purchase, and the buyer's signature;
  3. keep poisons in a separate locked cupboard, in containers labelled **"POISON"** with the name of the substance;
  4. not sell to children or to persons who appear intoxicated or unsound of mind.

### Import of poisons

The **Central Government** may regulate or prohibit the **import of any poison** into India by sea, air or land, and may allow import only under a licence.

### Search and seizure

A magistrate may issue a warrant to search a place where a poison is believed to be kept against the Act, and seize the poison.

### Penalties

Breaking the Act or rules is punishable with **fine or imprisonment for a short term**, with heavier punishment for a second offence. Poisons possessed against the Act may be confiscated. Exact amounts are in the 1919 Act and State rules; **check the current rules of your State**.

## 5.10 NDPS Act and Poisons Act compared

| Point | NDPS Act, 1985 | Poisons Act, 1919 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Substances | Narcotic drugs, psychotropics, precursors | Substances notified as poisons |
| Main concern | Addiction and trafficking | Accidental or deliberate poisoning |
| Detail made by | Mostly Central Act and rules, plus State rules | Mostly State rules |
| Punishment | Very strict, quantity-based | Light |
| International basis | Three UN conventions | None |

## Remember

- NDPS Act **1985** replaced the **Opium Acts (1857, 1878)** and the **Dangerous Drugs Act (1930)**; based on UN conventions of **1961, 1971 and 1988**.
- **Narcotic drug** = coca leaf, cannabis, opium, poppy straw and manufactured drugs; **psychotropic** = substances in the Schedule to the Act.
- **Charas** = resin; **ganja** = flowering tops.
- Authorities: **Narcotics Commissioner**, **NCB**, Consultative Committee, State Governments.
- Punishment depends on **small vs commercial quantity**; commercial quantity: **10–20 years** RI.
- **Essential narcotic drugs** (2014 amendment) improve access to pain relief.
- Poisons Act **1919**: import (Centre), possession and sale (State rules, licence, poison register).
